{{Short description|Loss function used in robust regression}}
In [[statistics]], the '''Huber loss''' is a [[loss function]] used in [[robust regression]], that is less sensitive to [[outlier]]s in data than the [[squared error loss]]. A variant for classification is also sometimes used.

==Definition==
[[File:Huber loss.svg|thumb|300px|Huber loss (green, <math>\delta=1</math>) and squared error loss (blue) as a function of <math>y - f(x)</math>]]
The Huber loss function describes the penalty incurred by an [[estimator|estimation procedure]] {{mvar|f}}. [[Peter J. Huber|Huber]] (1964) defines the loss function piecewise by<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Huber |first=Peter J. |author-link=Peter J. Huber|year=1964 |title=Robust Estimation of a Location Parameter |journal=[[Annals of Statistics]] |volume=53 |issue=1 |pages=73–101 |jstor=2238020 |doi=10.1214/aoms/1177703732|doi-access=free }}</ref>
<math display="block">
L_\delta (a) = \begin{cases}
 \frac{1}{2}{a^2}                   & \text{for } |a| \le \delta, \\[4pt]
 \delta \cdot \left(|a| - \frac{1}{2}\delta\right), & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
</math>

This function is quadratic for small values of {{mvar|a}}, and linear for large values, with equal values and slopes of the different sections at the two points where <math>|a| = \delta</math>. The variable {{mvar|a}} often refers to the residuals, that is to the difference between the observed and predicted values <math>a = y - f(x)</math>, so the former can be expanded to<ref>{{cite book |first1=Trevor |last1=Hastie |first2=Robert |last2=Tibshirani |first3=Jerome |last3=Friedman |year=2009 |title=The Elements of Statistical Learning |url=http://statweb.stanford.edu/~tibs/ElemStatLearn/ |page=349 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150126123924/http://statweb.stanford.edu/~tibs/ElemStatLearn/ |archive-date=2015-01-26 }} Compared to Hastie ''et al.'', the loss is scaled by a factor of {{sfrac|1|2}}, to be consistent with Huber's original definition given earlier.</ref>

<math display="block">
L_\delta(y, f(x)) = \begin{cases}
 \frac{1}{2} {\left(y - f(x)\right)}^2                   & \text{for } \left|y - f(x)\right| \le \delta, \\[4pt]
 \delta\ \cdot \left(\left|y - f(x)\right| - \frac{1}{2}\delta\right), & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
</math>

The Huber loss is the [[convolution]] of the [[absolute value]] function with the [[rectangular function]], scaled and translated. Thus it "smoothens out" the former's corner at the origin.
[[File:Comparison of loss functions.png|thumb|Comparison of Huber loss with other loss functions used for robust regression.]]

==Motivation==
Two very commonly used loss functions are the [[mean squared error|squared loss]], <math>L(a) = a^2</math>, and the [[absolute deviation|absolute loss]], <math>L(a)=|a|</math>. The squared loss function results in an [[arithmetic mean]]-[[unbiased estimator]], and the absolute-value loss function results in a [[median]]-unbiased estimator (in the one-dimensional case, and a [[geometric median]]-unbiased estimator for the multi-dimensional case). The squared loss has the disadvantage that it has the tendency to be dominated by outliers—when summing over a set of <math>a</math>'s (as in <math display="inline">\sum_{i=1}^n L(a_i) </math>), the sample mean is influenced too much by a few particularly large <math>a</math>-values when the distribution is heavy tailed: in terms of [[estimation theory]], the asymptotic relative efficiency of the mean is poor for heavy-tailed distributions.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Géron |first=Aurélien |title=Hands-On Machine Learning with Scikit-Learn, Keras & TensorFlow |date= |publisher=O'Reily |year=2023 |isbn=978-1-098-12597-4 |edition=3rd |publication-date=October 20, 2023 |pages=314,412}}</ref>

As defined above, the Huber loss function is [[convex function#Strongly convex functions|strongly convex]] in a uniform neighborhood of its minimum <math>a=0</math>; at the boundary of this uniform neighborhood, the Huber loss function has a differentiable extension to an affine function at points <math> a=-\delta </math> and <math> a = \delta </math>. These properties allow it to combine much of the sensitivity of the mean-unbiased, minimum-variance estimator of the mean (using the quadratic loss function) and the robustness of the median-unbiased estimator (using the absolute value function).

==Pseudo-Huber loss function==

The '''Pseudo-Huber loss function''' can be used as a [[Smoothness|smooth]] approximation of the Huber loss function. It combines the best properties of  '''L2''' [[Mean squared error|squared loss]] and '''L1''' [[Absolute deviation|absolute loss]] by being strongly convex when close to the target/minimum and less steep for extreme values. The scale at which the Pseudo-Huber loss function transitions from '''L2''' loss for values close to the minimum to '''L1''' loss for extreme values and the steepness at extreme values can be controlled by the <math>\delta</math> value. The '''Pseudo-Huber loss function''' ensures that derivatives are continuous for all degrees. It is defined as<ref>{{cite journal |first1=P. |last1=Charbonnier |first2=L. |last2=Blanc-Féraud |author2-link=Laure Blanc-Féraud|first3=G. |last3=Aubert |first4=M. |last4=Barlaud |title=Deterministic edge-preserving regularization in computed imaging |journal=IEEE Trans. Image Process. |year=1997 |volume=6 |issue=2 |pages=298–311 |doi=10.1109/83.551699|pmid=18282924 |bibcode=1997ITIP....6..298C |citeseerx=10.1.1.64.7521 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |first1=R. |last1=Hartley |first2=A. |last2=Zisserman |title=Multiple View Geometry in Computer Vision |url=https://archive.org/details/multipleviewgeom00hart_833 |url-access=limited |edition=2nd |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2003 |isbn=978-0-521-54051-3 |page=[https://archive.org/details/multipleviewgeom00hart_833/page/n634 619] }}</ref>

<math display="block">L_\delta (a) = \delta^2\left(\sqrt{1+(a/\delta)^2}-1\right).</math>

As such, this function approximates <math>a^2/2</math> for small values of <math>a</math>, and approximates a straight line with slope <math>\delta</math> for large values of <math>a</math>.

While the above is the most common form, other smooth approximations of the Huber loss function also exist.<ref>{{cite journal |first=K. |last=Lange |title=Convergence of Image Reconstruction Algorithms with Gibbs Smoothing |journal=IEEE Trans. Med. Imaging |year=1990 |volume=9 |issue=4 |pages=439–446 |doi=10.1109/42.61759|pmid=18222791 }}</ref>

==Variant for classification==
For [[statistical classification|classification]] purposes, a variant of the Huber loss called ''modified Huber'' is sometimes used. Given a prediction <math>f(x)</math> (a real-valued classifier score) and a true [[binary classification|binary]] class label <math>y \in \{+1, -1\}</math>, the modified Huber loss is defined as<ref name="zhang">{{cite conference |last=Zhang |first=Tong |title=Solving large scale linear prediction problems using stochastic gradient descent algorithms |conference=ICML |year=2004|url=https://dl.acm.org/citation.cfm?id=1015332}}</ref>

<math display="block">
L(y, f(x)) = \begin{cases}
 \max(0, 1 - y \, f(x))^2 & \text{for }\, \,  y \, f(x) > -1, \\[4pt]
 -4y \, f(x)              & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
</math>

The term <math>\max(0, 1 - y \, f(x))</math> is the [[hinge loss]] used by [[support vector machine]]s; the [[Hinge loss#Optimization|quadratically smoothed hinge loss]] is a generalization of <math>L</math>.<ref name="zhang"/>

==Applications==
The Huber loss function is used in [[robust statistics]],  [[M-estimator|M-estimation]] and [[additive model]]ling.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Friedman |first=J. H. |title=Greedy Function Approximation: A Gradient Boosting Machine |journal=[[Annals of Statistics]] |volume=26 |issue=5 |year=2001 |pages=1189–1232 |jstor=2699986 |doi=10.1214/aos/1013203451|doi-access=free }}</ref>
